segments.say: Many people spend a large part of their waking life at work. And for some, work is where boredom hits hardest. Repetitive tasks. Long meetings. Paperwork. Waiting for others. Projects with no clear purpose. It's not unusual to hear people say, I'm so bored at work, as if it were simply part of the deal.

Researchers who study work often distinguish between overload, too much to do, and underload, too little challenge. Burnout, from overload, gets a lot of attention. But some writers have described a less discussed problem, sometimes called boreout. Chronic boredom at work, from too little challenge, too little meaning, or too little to do.

Interestingly, boredom at work can be exhausting, even though it involves less activity. People often report feeling drained at the end of a boring day, sometimes more than after a busy one. Fighting to stay focused on something that doesn't hold your attention takes effort. And the lack of meaning can weigh heavily on mood.

Some research has linked boredom at work to less helpful behaviors, like more distraction, more time spent on unrelated activities, and, in some studies, more counterproductive behavior. It's not that bored workers are bad people. It's that boredom, as we've seen, creates a strong craving for something to happen.

Organizational psychologists have long studied what makes work engaging. A well known model, developed by J. Richard Hackman and Greg Oldham in the nineteen seventies, highlighted several key features. Variety in tasks. Seeing a whole piece of work through from start to finish. Knowing that your work matters to others. Some autonomy. And feedback on how you're doing.

Many of these features can be improved, even in small ways. Mixing different tasks through the day, rather than doing one repetitive task for hours. Understanding how your work helps someone else. Having some say in how you do things. Getting feedback. Each of these can make work feel less boring, and more meaningful.

Researchers Amy Wrzesniewski and Jane Dutton described something they called job crafting. Small changes people make to their own jobs, to make them more meaningful. Changing which tasks they focus on. Changing how they relate to colleagues or customers. Or changing how they think about the purpose of their work. Even within the same job, people can craft a different experience.

In one of their well known studies, they described hospital cleaners who saw their work not just as cleaning, but as part of caring for patients. Some chatted with patients, helped families, and saw themselves as part of the healing team. The tasks were the same. But the meaning they found in them was very different, and so was their experience.

Of course, sometimes boredom at work is a sign that a job no longer fits. That you've outgrown it, or that it doesn't use your strengths or match your values. In those cases, boredom might be a useful nudge to look for new challenges, a new role, or new learning. Not every boredom can be crafted away.

If you're bored at work, it's not a personal failing. It may be a sign of a mismatch between you and your tasks. You can experiment with small changes, seek more variety or meaning, or ask for new challenges. And whatever you decide, you deserve work that engages you, at least some of the time.

So here's what we've learned about boredom at work. Too little challenge can be as draining as too much. Boredom at work fuels distraction and frustration. Variety, meaning, autonomy and feedback make work more engaging. And small changes, known as job crafting, can reshape how work feels, even within the same role.

segments.say: Boredom can also visit our closest relationships. After years together, couples can fall into comfortable routines, and sometimes into a quiet kind of boredom. Researchers have tested a simple way to bring back some spark.
